title: Binary Trees
relevance: Binary trees are a core hierarchical structure tested heavily in SDE interviews and OAs via traversals, structural checks, and recursive bottom-up patterns.

phases.goal: Establish what a binary tree is, its terminology, common shapes, and how DFS/BFS traversals are defined.

must_hit.point: A binary tree is hierarchical and each node has at most two children (left and right).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States at most two children and contrasts trees with linear structures like arrays or linked lists.

must_hit.point: Height is the longest path from a node to a leaf; depth is the path length from the root to a node.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly separates height (down to a leaf) from depth (from the root).

must_hit.point: Full means every node has 0 or 2 children; complete fills levels left-to-right except possibly the last; perfect has all internal nodes with two children and all leaves at the same level; balanced means left/right heights differ by at most 1; degenerate means every internal node has exactly one child.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names and distinguishes full, complete, perfect, balanced, and degenerate correctly.

must_hit.point: Preorder/inorder/postorder are DFS and differ only by when the node is processed: Node-Left-Right, Left-Node-Right, Left-Right-Node; BFS is level-order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the three DFS orders and contrasts them with level-by-level BFS.

must_hit.point: Trees may use array form (heap-style children at 2i+1 and 2i+2) or pointer/linked nodes; pointers are most common for arbitrary binary trees.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions both representations and that linked nodes are usual for arbitrary trees.

probes: What is a binary tree, and how do height and depth differ?
Define full, complete, perfect, balanced, and degenerate binary trees.
How do preorder, inorder, and postorder differ, and how does BFS fit in?

hints.1: Think about node degree and hierarchical terminology first.
hints.2: Separate shape definitions from traversal visit orders.
hints.3: Preorder=NLR, inorder=LNR, postorder=LRN; BFS walks level by level with a queue.

phases.goal: Show how recursive and iterative traversals work, plus the bottom-up DFS and parent-map patterns used in classic tree problems.

must_hit.point: Recursive DFS traversals visit each node once in O(n) time with O(h) recursion-stack space (worst-case O(n), average O(log n) for balanced shapes).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives O(n) visits and O(h) stack, noting skewed vs average cases.

must_hit.point: Level-order BFS uses a queue and must capture size = queue.size() at the start of each loop to isolate one level; space can reach O(n) because a perfect tree level can hold n/2 nodes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions snapshotting queue size per level and widest-level queue occupancy.

must_hit.point: Iterative preorder uses an explicit stack and pushes right before left so LIFO processes left first; iterative inorder walks left while pushing, then pops/processes and moves right.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains right-first push for preorder and left-then-pop-then-right for inorder.

must_hit.point: Two-stack postorder builds Node-Right-Left then reverses via a second stack (O(n) space); one-stack postorder tracks lastProcessed to know whether the right child is done (O(h) space).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts reverse-via-second-stack with last-processed one-stack control.

must_hit.point: A single iterative pass can emit pre/in/post by treating each node as a 3-state machine (state 1 pre, 2 in, 3 post), visiting each node 3 times.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes stack pairs of node+state and the three visit moments.

must_hit.point: Bottom-up postorder returns child info upward: empty height is 0; max depth is 1 + max(left,right); balance can return -1 as a sentinel while computing height; diameter through a node is leftHeight + rightHeight.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties height base case, depth formula, -1 imbalance signal, and diameter as sum of child heights.

probes: Walk through recursive preorder/inorder/postorder and their complexities.
How do you implement level-order so each level is grouped correctly?
How would you do iterative preorder and inorder with a stack?
How can one DFS pass check balance or compute diameter while returning height?

hints.1: Start from the recursive visit order, then replace the call stack with an explicit stack or queue.
hints.2: For BFS, freeze the current level length before pushing children; for structural metrics, return height from children first.
hints.3: Empty -> height 0; balanced check propagates -1; diameter updates with leftHeight + rightHeight at each node.

phases.goal: Compare representation choices and recursive vs iterative/space-optimized approaches called out in the material.

must_hit.point: Array representation suits heap-like complete shapes with index arithmetic, while pointer/linked nodes are preferred for arbitrary binary trees.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says arrays are common for heaps and pointers for arbitrary trees.

must_hit.point: Naive per-node height checks for balance or diameter take O(N^2); combining the check with bottom-up height computation reduces them to O(N).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States brute O(N^2) vs single-pass O(N) with height reuse / -1 sentinel.

must_hit.point: Two-stack iterative postorder is simpler but uses O(n) space via st2; one-stack postorder uses O(h) but needs lastProcessed bookkeeping.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares O(n) second-stack storage against O(h) one-stack control complexity.

must_hit.point: Morris inorder/preorder achieve O(1) extra space by temporarily threading predecessor right pointers, versus O(h) recursion or explicit-stack DFS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names temporary threads from inorder predecessor and O(1) auxiliary space.

must_hit.point: Counting nodes in a complete tree can be O(n) by visiting all nodes, or O(log^2 n) by short-circuiting perfect subtrees of height h as 2^h - 1 nodes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses equal left/right extreme heights to apply 2^h - 1 and recurse otherwise.

probes: When would you store a binary tree in an array versus with child pointers?
Why is the naive balanced/diameter approach quadratic, and how do you make it linear?
What do you gain and lose moving from recursive DFS to Morris traversal?

hints.1: Think about completeness/heap indexing versus arbitrary shapes.
hints.2: Reuse height already computed on the way up instead of recomputing per node.
hints.3: Morris threads predecessor->right temporarily for O(1) space; complete-tree counting uses 2^h - 1 on perfect subtrees.

phases.goal: Apply traversal and bottom-up patterns to standard medium/hard interview problems from the file.

must_hit.point: Maximum path sum allows negative values, so discard negative subtree contributions with max(0, subtreeMaxPath); a path may turn at a node using val + left + right as a global candidate while returning only one side upward.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions clamping negatives to 0 and splitting arch update vs upward return.

must_hit.point: LCA: if root is null/p/q return root; if left and right searches both nonempty, root is LCA; otherwise propagate the nonempty side; a node may be a descendant of itself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the both-sides-non-null rule and self-descendant allowance.

must_hit.point: Views: top view keeps the first BFS node per column; bottom view overwrites so the last remains; right view can take the last node per BFS level or DFS right-before-left when depth equals result size.
must_hit.evidence_hint: First vs last per column for top/bottom; last-per-level or right-first DFS for right view.

must_hit.point: Distance-k / burn-tree style problems map parents first, then BFS radially through left, right, and parent; burn time is the number of BFS expansion levels until the queue empties.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes parent map then multi-direction BFS; time increments per burned level.

must_hit.point: Construction: preorder’s first (or postorder’s last) element is the root; inorder splits left/right sizes; serialize/deserialize can encode nulls (e.g. #) in level-order BFS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Root from preorder first/postorder last, inorder partition, and BFS string with null markers.

must_hit.point: Maximum width assigns indices with left 2i+1 and right 2i+2, measures last-first+1 including nulls between ends, and normalizes indices per level to avoid overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States heap-style indexing, width formula, and per-level index normalization.

probes: How do you compute maximum path sum when node values can be negative?
Find the LCA of two nodes in a general binary tree.
How do top, bottom, and right views differ in what you keep per column or level?
How would you reconstruct a tree from preorder+inorder or serialize it?

hints.1: Most hard tree answers return child state upward or BFS with extra metadata.
hints.2: For path/LCA/balance-style problems use postorder returns; for distance/views/width use BFS plus maps or indices.
hints.3: Path sum clamps negatives and updates on a turn; LCA returns root when both sides hit; construction uses preorder/postorder root + inorder split.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays with children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 fit heaps/complete layouts; pointer nodes are the usual choice for arbitrary binary trees.

tradeoffs.topic: Brute per-node height checks vs bottom-up single DFS
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Recomputing height at every node is O(N^2) for balance/diameter; returning height (and a -1 imbalance sentinel) in one postorder pass is O(N).
Two stacks generate Node-Right-Left then reverse with O(n) space on st2; one stack uses O(h) space but must track lastProcessed to avoid re-entering the right child.
Normal DFS uses O(h) stack space; Morris temporarily threads the inorder predecessor’s right pointer to get O(1) extra space, then removes the thread.

tradeoffs.topic: Naive node count vs complete-tree height short-circuit
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Visiting all nodes is O(n); in a complete tree, equal leftmost/rightmost heights mean a perfect subtree of 2^h - 1 nodes, giving O(log^2 n) overall.

gotchas.trap: In level-order, mixing nodes from adjacent levels in one loop pass.
gotchas.correction: Capture size = queue.size() at the start of each iteration and only process that many nodes as the current level.

gotchas.trap: Treating an empty tree’s height as undefined or nonzero when writing recursive depth/balance code.
gotchas.correction: The height of a nullptr / empty tree is 0 and is the recursion base case.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the diameter always passes through the root.
gotchas.correction: Diameter is the longest path between any two nodes and may lie entirely in a subtree; track max(leftHeight + rightHeight) at every node.

gotchas.trap: Including negative subtree sums in maximum path sum.
gotchas.correction: Take max(0, subtreeMaxPath) so a negative branch is dropped; still allow a path to turn using val + left + right for the global answer.

gotchas.trap: Pushing left before right on an iterative preorder stack.
gotchas.correction: Because a stack is LIFO, push right first, then left, so left is processed first.

gotchas.trap: Using only downward child pointers for distance-k or burn-tree problems.
gotchas.correction: First build a parent map so BFS can move to left, right, and parent; mark visited to avoid revisiting.

gotchas.trap: Trying to reconstruct a unique binary tree from a single traversal.
gotchas.correction: One traversal alone is insufficient; need one sequence that identifies the root and another (inorder) that partitions left/right subtree sizes.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting that Morris traversal mutates the tree while running.
gotchas.correction: It creates temporary predecessor-to-current right threads and must clear them when revisited so the structure is restored.
